sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819

items.q: Acid–base balance matters because four listed functions work well only across a narrow pH range. Which set?
opts: Enzyme system, muscle and nerve, oxygenation and metabolic function
Clotting cascade, thermoregulation, gut motility and immune surveillance
Enzyme system, hormonal synthesis, bone turnover and drug metabolism
Oxygenation, oncotic pressure, cardiac conduction and vitamin activation
items.exp: Acid–base balance matters for the enzyme system, muscle and nerve, oxygenation and metabolic function — all of which function well only across a narrow pH range. (Book p819)

items.q: Per day H⁺ production, as quantified at the start of the chapter, is:
items.exp: Per day H⁺ production is given as 7 crore nmol (= 70 mmol of fixed acid), while the blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is 40 nmol/L. (Book p819)

items.q: Blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is:
items.exp: Blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is 40 nmol/L; the daily acid load of 7 crore nmol is far larger, which is why buffering is needed. (Book p819)

items.q: Match the fate of excess H⁺ as printed — 1) Excess H⁺  2) Its cellular effect  3) Final outcome … A) Rendered safe by the buffering system  B) Alters cellular morphology  C) Cellulotoxic
items.exp: Excess H⁺ → cellulotoxic → alters cellular morphology → rendered safe by buffering system. (Book p819)

items.q: ‘Excess H⁺ is made harmless by altering cellular morphology, without any buffering.’
opts: False — the buffering system renders the H⁺ safe; morphology change is the toxic step
True — morphological change is the neutralising step
True, as long as renal acid excretion is intact
False — H⁺ is removed only by alveolar ventilation
items.exp: The arrow is the other way round: excess H⁺ is cellulotoxic and alters cellular morphology, and is then rendered safe by the buffering system. (Book p819)

items.q: Match the buffering system to its printed response time — 1) Chemical  2) Respiratory  3) Renal … A) Slow response  B) Immediate response  C) Fast response
items.exp: Buffering system types: chemical = immediate response, respiratory = fast response, renal = slow response. (Book p819)

items.q: Fill up: The most potent extracellular buffering system is ______.
items.exp: [H⁺] + [HCO₃⁻] → H₂CO₃ is labelled the most potent extracellular buffering system. (Book p819)

items.q: The general chemical buffering reaction is written as:
items.exp: Chemical buffering: [H⁺] + [A⁻] (conjugate base) → HA (acid); the particular case with A⁻ = HCO₃⁻ is the most potent extracellular buffer. (Book p819)

items.q: Fill up: pKa is the pH at which ______.
opts: pH equals the PaCO₂ in mmHg
items.exp: pKa is the pH at which acid state is 50% [A⁻] = 50% [HA]. (Book p819)

items.q: The mechanism of chemical buffering is expressed by which equation?
items.exp: pH = pKa + log [A⁻] (conjugate base) / [HA] (acid) — the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation as printed under ‘mechanism’. (Book p819)

items.q: ‘A strong acid (pKa < 3) exists more in the HA form and is therefore not good for basic functions.’
opts: True — existing mainly as HA makes strong acids poor buffers
False — strong acids exist mainly as A⁻ and are the best buffers
True — and weak acids also exist mainly as HA
False — pKa < 3 means the acid exists only as A⁻
items.exp: Strong acid (pKa < 3) exists more in [HA] form: not good for basic functions. (Book p819)

items.q: Which acids are called the best buffer system, and why?
opts: Weak acids — they exist more in the [A⁻] form
Strong acids — they exist more in the [HA] form
Weak acids — they exist more in the [HA] form
Strong acids — they exist more in the [A⁻] form
items.exp: Weak acids exist more in the [A⁻] form and are therefore the best buffer system, unlike strong acids (pKa < 3) which sit mainly as HA. (Book p819)

items.q: All but one of the following chemical buffers are named in the Book. Which is the odd one out?
items.exp: The three chemical buffers printed are the HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ system, the phosphate buffer and the haemoglobin buffer; an ammonium pair is not listed as a chemical buffer. (Book p819)
